summary: Specifies new HMAC-SHA-2 authentication protocols for the User-based Security Model (USM) of SNMPv3, which was defined in RFC 3414. They add stronger hash-based options for authenticating management messages. It was replaced by RFC 7860.

plainLanguage.summary: A secret stamp proves a message really came from the right sender. This gives network management messages a stronger stamp. It was replaced by RFC 7860.

subtitle: Stronger hash-based authentication for network management messages using SHA-2 instead of older hashes.

tldr.problem: SNMPv3 authentication was originally limited to MD5 and SHA-1, both considered weak or aging by 2015 standards.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7630 defines four new HMAC-SHA-2 authentication protocols for SNMPv3's User-based Security Model, using SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 with appropriate truncation.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators can now use stronger cryptographic authentication for SNMP management traffic, though this RFC was replaced by RFC 7860.

today: RFC 7630 is a Standards Track document from October 2015, but it has been superseded by RFC 7860, which consolidates and updates the SNMPv3 authentication and encryption protocols.

sections.title: Stronger Authentication for Network Management
sections.content:
RFC 7630 extends SNMPv3's User-based Security Model (USM) defined in RFC 3414 with four new HMAC-SHA-2 authentication protocols. The original SNMPv3 authentication used HMAC-MD5-96 and HMAC-SHA-96, both based on weaker or older hash functions.

These new protocols add support for the SHA-2 family of hash functions (SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512), each truncated to an appropriate output size for use in the SNMP protocol. This allows network administrators to apply stronger cryptographic authentication to their management traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is a way to manage network equipment. SNMPv3 lets you prove your identity with a secret code. This document adds newer, stronger secret codes based on modern cryptography.

sections.title: The Four SHA-2 Authentication Protocols
sections.content:
RFC 7630 defines four protocols, each using a different SHA-2 hash function and truncation length. The usmHMAC192SHA256AuthProtocol uses SHA-256 and truncates the output to 192 bits (24 octets), and implementations MUST support this protocol. The usmHMAC384SHA512AuthProtocol uses SHA-512 truncated to 384 bits (48 octets) and SHOULD be supported.

Two additional optional protocols are defined: usmHMAC128SHA224AuthProtocol (SHA-224 truncated to 128 bits or 16 octets) and usmHMAC256SHA384AuthProtocol (SHA-384 truncated to 256 bits or 32 octets). Each protocol derives its secret key using the same hash function.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four versions, each using a different strength of SHA-2 encryption. The medium-strength versions (SHA-256 and SHA-512) are the important ones; others are optional.

sections.title: Key Differences from Older Protocols
sections.content:
These protocols differ from the older HMAC-MD5-96 and HMAC-SHA-96 in three main ways. First, they use SHA-2 hash functions instead of MD5 or SHA-1. Second, the message digest output is longer before truncation: 224, 256, 384, or 512 bits depending on the protocol, versus the 160-bit SHA-1 or 128-bit MD5 previously used. Third, the truncation is deeper: between 128 and 384 bits in the output, whereas the older protocols truncated to just 96 bits.

As a result, the secret key used for each protocol must also be longer: 28 octets for SHA-224, 32 for SHA-256, 48 for SHA-384, and 64 for SHA-512, compared to 16 or 20 octets in the older protocols. The key length is derived from a password using the same SHA-2 hash function selected for the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: The new protocols use stronger building blocks and longer secret codes than the old ones. This makes them harder to break.

sections.title: How Authentication Works
sections.content:
When an SNMP engine sends an authenticated message, it computes an HMAC using the secret key and the appropriate SHA-2 function, then truncates the output and includes those bytes in the msgAuthenticationParameters field. When a message arrives, the engine checks that the received authentication code matches the code computed over the message.

The process follows the same steps as HMAC-SHA-96 from RFC 3414, with the hash function and truncation lengths adjusted. The SNMP message is treated as a whole, and the computed MAC is placed in the message before transmission. A receiver recalculates the MAC and compares it to the one received to verify authenticity.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender stamps the message with a secret code computed using SHA-2. The receiver checks the stamp using the same secret, and if they match, the message is real.

sections.title: Cryptographic Strength and Key Derivation
sections.content:
At the time of publication, all four HMAC-SHA-2 authentication protocols provided a very high level of security. The strength depends on the key length (if the key has maximum entropy), the hash function's internal state size, and the truncated MAC length. For example, usmHMAC192SHA256AuthProtocol uses a 256-bit key with a 256-bit internal state and a 192-bit truncated output.

If secret keys are derived from passwords, the derivation SHOULD use the password-to-key algorithm from RFC 3414 Appendix A.1, replacing MD5 with the appropriate SHA-2 function. The password is hashed into a 1,048,576-octet string, then combined with the SNMP engine ID. This process ensures that keys derived from short passwords are still long enough to provide security.
sections.plainLanguage: Longer secret codes and stronger math inside make these protocols very hard to break. If you use a password, it gets stretched to make sure the secret code is strong.
